notes: \cpara{Recalls the first rung of a ladder of virtues: ``tsuyoku naritai'' (``I want to become stronger''), from the post of that name earlier in the book.}
\cpara{The second rung, ``make a desperate effort,'' from the previous day's post, ``Make an Extraordinary Effort,'' with a line from \textsc{Flashing Steel}, a book on swordsmanship quoted there.}
\cpara{The third rung, from the same post: leave your comfort zone and accept the risk of going ``outside the System.''}
\cpara{Asks the question the post answers: what if even that is not enough?}

\cpara{Recalls the author's younger self calling four problems impossible. This agrees with ``On Doing the Impossible,'' two days earlier, where the author says of understanding intelligence precisely: ``Originally, I'd written off this problem as impossible''.}
\cpara{Introduces the title as the message the author would send back to that younger self.}

\cpara{Justifies the message. ``Impossible'' usually means ``I see no way to do this,'' not a proof, and such a problem may seem less impossible after a year or five of study. This is the distinction ``On Doing the Impossible'' drew between a proof of impossibility and ``I can't see any way to do that.''}
\cpara{Says the principle is subtler than that, and sets ``Try to do the impossible'' against the title.}

\cpara{Chooses the one example, the AI-Box Experiment, and calls it the ``least impossible impossibility'' the author has accomplished. The experiment's rules, and its page's own description of the results as ``strictly anecdotal evidence,'' are given in the notes on ``Einstein's Superpowers.''}
\cpara{Tells how the experiment began: once more, someone proposed keeping an AI isolated so that it could do no harm.}
\cpara{Gives the standard reply: humans are not secure systems, so a superintelligence would persuade its keeper to let it out.}
\cpara{The objection that led to the first game. The quoted sentence matches, word for word, Nathan Russell's first message to the SL4 mailing list (7 March 2002).}
\cpara{The author's reply, which also matches the SL4 archive (8 March 2002), shortened without change of sense. The secrecy rule and its reason were stated before the first game was played.}

\cpara{The result does not rest on the author's word alone. On 8 March 2002 Russell posted a signed message to the list: ``I decided to let Eliezer out.'' Under the secrecy rule just quoted, the conversation itself was not released.}

\cpara{The second game (July 2002, with David McFadzean, for \$20). The two remarks quoted here as one come from the chat log the author posted to SL4 on 4 July 2002, with other lines between them; the exchange about a transhuman AI matches the log. McFadzean confirmed the result in a signed message the next day: ``I let the transhuman AI out of the box.''}
\cpara{Introduces four comments from the Something Awful forums, forwarded to the author. The link goes to the experiment's page, which does not carry them. I could not find the thread.}
\cpara{The four comments: disbelief that anyone would give in with \$10 at stake, awe at the author, and the suggestion that the tests were faked.}
\cpara{A joke, and a return to the argument.}
\cpara{Says these readers find the experiment impossible even after being told it happened, and are tempted to ``deny the data.''}
\cpara{Asks readers who find the Box easy to imagine it as absurd as it seemed to the commenters. The author will not use a really impossible example.}
\cpara{Compares the Box with ``a reductionist decomposition of consciousness'' and calls it about ``as easy as a problem can get'' while still being impossible.}
\cpara{Sets the reader the challenge.}
\cpara{First step: do not give up at once, as Luke Skywalker does in the post linked, ``Use the Try Harder, Luke.''}
\cpara{Gives reasons to stay: a trained habit, a threat to your daughter, or pride. Something must be at stake.}
\cpara{Tests the first virtue against the Box: growing stronger over many tries may be too slow, and ``sometimes a single failure isn't acceptable.''}
\cpara{Adds that even picturing a better second try begins to bind you to the problem, and asks how to do better by skill.}
\cpara{Tests the second virtue: more effort along known lines does not help when no known line leads to a solution.}
\cpara{Tests the third: a few minutes of creative brainstorming can count as leaving your comfort zone, and still fail.}
\cpara{The answer to all three.}
\cpara{Gives the reason, from ``Trying to Try'' a week earlier: making an effort is a different goal from winning, and can be met while losing.}
\cpara{Voices the objection in the words ``Trying to Try'' gave to the author's own earlier view of Yoda: ``SUCCEED is not a primitive action.''}
\cpara{Grants the objection and repeats the command.}
\cpara{States the goal: to get out of the box.}
\cpara{Names the ``awful tension'' between the impossibility and the demand, and says people try to escape it.}

\cpara{Reports two guesses about how the author won: a threat, or an offer of a trillion dollars, made inside the game. The author replies that a sensible gatekeeper would keep saying no. The author's protocol allows such offers inside the game (``The AI may offer the Gatekeeper the moon and the stars on a diamond chain'') and forbids real ones.}
\cpara{Says such guessers are trying too hard to convince themselves that the problem is not impossible.}
\cpara{The first way of escaping the tension: seize any solution, even a poor one.}
\cpara{Hence the need for a true intent to produce a good solution and win.}
\cpara{Rejects the other remedy: raising your own estimate of success would achieve nothing, and might lead you to a merely desperate effort.}
\cpara{Faith in success would be another way of escaping the tension.}
\cpara{Restates ``Trying to Try'': set out to win, not to try or to do your best.}
\cpara{Says it again: you must intend to solve the problem. If you believe you will fail, your search ends in ``Oh well.''}

\clogic{Stated without evidence, but the nearest research I found agrees. Oettingen and Mayer (2002) report that ``Positive expectations (judging a desired future as likely) predicted high effort and successful performance.'' In a related study, people who weighed a desired future against present obstacles committed strongly only ``in light of favorable expectations'' (Oettingen, Pak and Schnetter, 2001). I read the abstracts only.}
\cpara{The reply to ``Oh well.''}

\cpara{Turns to AI researchers who call Friendly AI impossible. That they ``haven't even tried for the sake of trying'' is offered with ``I'm pretty sure,'' about unnamed people, with no example. What they would do if they tried for five minutes, and why (``to make themselves defensible''), is asserted on the same basis.}
\cpara{Asks whether this means doublethink: making yourself believe you will surely win, or even raising your honest estimate at all.}
\cpara{Answers no: keep in full view why you cannot succeed, or you will ``seize on a false solution.''}
\cpara{A rule of thumb, offered with ``often'': if you can say exactly why something is impossible, you are often close to a solution.}
\cpara{The central instruction: hold both views at once, the full impossibility and the intent to solve.}

\cpara{Places the tension in not knowing which view will win, and says to refuse even the relief of accepting uncertainty. The closing words, ``unknown to death, nor known to life,'' are from Archer's incantation in the visual novel \textsc{Fate/stay night} (2004), as Know Your Meme quotes it.}

\cpara{Says fiction rarely shows an attempt at the impossible with the outcome truly in doubt. ``Bambi choosing to take on Godzilla'' and ``the default squish'' refer to \textsc{Bambi Meets Godzilla} (1969), a 92-second cartoon in which Godzilla's foot comes down on Bambi.}
\cpara{Allows that one may refuse to use probabilities here. The author says plainly that they cannot estimate the chance of solving an impossible problem they have set out to solve.}
\cpara{Applies this to human survival and Friendly AI: the author does not know how to put a number on success, and calls any estimate ``wildly unstable.''}
\cpara{Declares, in the post's sense of the word, that building a Friendly AI is impossible.}

\cpara{Explains the author's response to proposals for safe AI. The specific flaws would each be ``a whole long story'' (the link is to ``Dreams of Friendliness''); the general rule is that a proposal needing only ordinary effort deserves suspicion.}
\cpara{Introduces the one hint the author has given about the Box. The reply quoted matches, word for word, the author's comment on Hacker News of 21 May 2008.}

\cpara{Repeats the hint and adds that there was no bribe or other breach of the experiment's spirit. The protocol page says the same of the two 2002 games: ``I (Yudkowsky) obeyed this protocol voluntarily in both earlier tests.''}
\cpara{Concedes that the Box never seemed impossible to the author, and says that failing to think of a convincing argument only means a search ``hasn't yet turned up a path.''}

\cpara{Draws the point the example illustrates: doing the impossible is not finding a cheap way out. On how the games were won, the reader has only the author's report, since by the rules the post quoted their content is secret.}
\cpara{Ranks the four virtues by what they cost the person who uses them.}
\cpara{Describes the state of mind: the wall, both awarenesses at once, and moving forward ``like walking through concrete.''}
\cpara{Says to lower the cost of the tension where possible, and to take a real shortcut if there is one; the author has found none.}
\cpara{Reports three further games, for stakes of up to thousands of dollars: one won, two lost. The record in the post is three wins in five games.}

\cfact{I found no other first-hand record of these three games. As the post says, they were never added to the AI-Box page, which still reads ``So far, this test has actually been run on two occasions'' (checked September 2026); RationalWiki's account cites this post. Others later played the game and reported the results. One, writing as Tuxedage on LessWrong, used the author's rules in a first game in January 2013, lost as the AI, and by December reported a record of ``3 Wins, 3 Losses.''}
\cpara{Describes what the losses cost the author.}
\cpara{Calls the author a sore loser, and says this drives the work on impossible problems.}
\cpara{Warns that losing is ``allowed to happen'' (the link is to ``Beyond the Reach of God'') and costs time and resources.}
\cpara{Reserves the method for very special occasions, as ``On Doing the Impossible'' did: ``Doing the impossible should be reserved for very special occasions.''}
\cpara{Ends: only at this level do ``adult problems'' come into sight.}
